question:
The following sentence has two blanks. Choose the most suitable set of prepositions from the given options to fill in the blanks and complete the sentence meaningfully.

My cousin lives ____ carter road ____ the bank.
solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. on, next to.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence describes a location where the cousin lives in relation to Carter Road and a bank.
 
• The correct preposition for describing a residence on a street is **"on"**. For proximity to another landmark, **"next to"** is appropriate.
 
• Options such as **"at"** are incorrect because "at" is typically used for specific points or locations rather than streets.
 
• Similarly, "besides" and "beside" are less commonly used in this context compared to "next to" for indicating proximity.

Correct sentence: *My cousin lives **on** Carter Road **next to** the bank.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Usage of Prepositions:**

 
 
• **On:** Used to indicate a position on a surface or street (e.g., "on Carter Road").
 
• **Next to:** Indicates a position immediately adjacent to something (e.g., "next to the bank").
 
• **At:** Refers to a specific point or location (e.g., "at the corner").
 
• **Beside/Besides:** Beside means "next to" but is less common in modern usage for locations, while besides means "in addition to" and is unrelated to physical positioning.

subject: ENG
question:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

Mahesh said to the interviewer, "Sir, I was in charge of the production unit at my previous office."

options.text: Mahesh told the interviewer that Sir was in charge of the production unit at my previous office.
Mahesh told the interviewer that he had been in charge of the production unit at his previous office.
Mahesh told the interviewer you were in charge of the production unit at my previous office.
Mahesh told the interviewer I was in charge of the production unit at his previous office.

solution:
The correct answer is** option 2) i.e. Mahesh told the interviewer that he had been in charge of the production unit at his previous office.**

__
 
• While changing direct speech into indirect speech** said to** is changed into **told**.
 
• And** 'I'** is referred to **Mahesh**, hence, 'I' will be changed into **'he'**.
 
• The tense of the reported speech (here:** Simple past)** would undergo a** backshift **(get changed into** Past perfect) i.e. 'was/were'** would be changed into **'had been' **and** V2 would be changed into V3.**
 
• All these rules are followed in option 2, hence, it will be the correct answer.

NOTE: __When a sentence is converted from Direct speech into Indirect speech:

 
• If the 'reporting verb' is in 'Past tense', the 'Reported speech' would undergo a backshift of tense.
 
• Modal verbs (Will, may, can) would take their past forms (would, might, could).
 
• Pronouns would change according to the subject of reporting verb.​
 
• "said to" will get converted to "told", "asked", "commanded", requested" etc.depending on the tone of the narrator.

 __

 Present simple (Subject + V1st + Object)

__
 
• The following changes occur when an** interrogative sentence** in the **direct speech** is changed to the** indirect speech**:

 
 
• **Inverted commas ('' '') **and **question mark (?**) will be **removed**.
 
 
 
• The **simple past tense** of the sentence (**Subject+v2+object)** will change into** past perfect tense** **(Subject+had+v3+object).**

 She said that Gautam **had arrived **on Sunday. (***Indirect***)

 
• **No conjunction** is used, if a sentence in **direct speech** **begins** with a **question** (**what/where/when**) as the “question-word” itself acts as a **joining clause**.
 
• **Reporting verbs** such as ‘**said/ said to’** changes to** enquired, asked, or demanded.**
 
• While changing **direct speech to indirect speech,** the **modals** used in the sentences change like: **can become could, may become might, etc.**
 
• The** first person** in **direct speech** changes as per the **subject** of the speech.
 
• The **second person **of **direct speech **changes as per the **object** of reporting speech.
 
• The** third person** of **direct speech doesn’t change. **
 
• In the given sentence '**their**' is the **third person **therefore** no changes** will be made.
 
• Hence, keeping all the rules in mind it can be concluded that** option 4** is the **correct answer.**

 

**The correct sentence:**__ *The sports coach asked the class prefect where the children had left their record books.*

• When converting a sentence from** direct to indirect speech,** we need to make some changes to the original sentence.
 
• Here are the rules:
 
 
• The reporting verb (said) is changed to a reporting clause (that + subject + verb).
 
• The pronouns and possessive adjectives are changed to reflect the new subject of the sentence.
 
• The tense of the verb is usually shifted back one tense (present becomes past, past becomes past perfect).
 
• Time and place expressions may need to be changed.
 
 
 
• Using these rules, we can convert the given sentence from direct to indirect speech:
 
• **Direct speech:** The sage said, "Man proposes and God disposes."
 
• **Indirect speech:** The sage said that man proposes and God disposes.
 
• The given reported speech is a general truth, therefore, there will be no change in the tense of the reported speech.
 
• Therefore, the correct answer is** option 1.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• To convert a direct speech sentence to indirect speech, we usually follow certain grammar rules.
 
• Here's the breakdown of the conversion for this particular sentence:
 
• The reporting verb** "said"** remains unchanged.
 
• **Commas and inverted commas** are removed and the conjunction **'that' **is added.
 
• The pronoun **"I"** is changed to the third-person pronoun **"she"** because we are reporting someone else's words.
 
• The verb tense undergoes a backshift. Since the original sentence is in the present tense **("am"),** it is changed to the past tense **("was")**.
 
• The phrase **"not invested"** remains the same.
 
• The phrase **"anymore"** remains the same.
 
• Now let's analyze why the correct answer is** option 3:**
 
• **Option 1: "Aditi said that she had not invested in the project anymore." **This option incorrectly uses the past perfect tense ("had not invested") instead of the simple past tense ("was not invested").
 
• **Option 2: "Aditi said that she is not invested in the project anymore."** This option uses the present tense ("is") instead of the past tense ("was").
 
• **Option 3: "Aditi said that she was not invested in the project anymore." **This option correctly follows the grammar rules by changing the verb tense to the past tense ("was") and maintains the correct structure and meaning of the original sentence.
 
• **Option 4: "Aditi said that she do not invested in the project anymore." **This option is grammatically incorrect because it uses "do not invested," which is an incorrect verb form.

• Therefore, when** we convert the indirect speech back to direct**, we **revert** this change.
 
• In the sentence "The teacher asked me if I had seen the match", the phrase **"had seen"** is in the **past perfect tense.**
 
• In direct speech, this would have been in the past simple tense, which is **"did see" **or more commonly expressed as** "did you see".**

Therefore, the **correct direct form **of the sentence: *"The teacher asked me if I had seen the match" is "Did you see the match?" the teacher said to me.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **"Did you saw the match?" the teacher said to me. - **This sentence is also grammatically incorrect. **After "did", we use the base form **of the verb, which is "see", not the past form "saw".

**Direction: Select the option that expresses the given sentence in positive degree of comparison.**

He was greater than any other physiologist of the century.

options.text: All other physiologists were as great as him.
He was the greatest physiologist of all.
He as a physiologist in the country was among the greatest people.
No other physiologist of the century was as great as he was.

solution:
The correct answer is **"No other physiologist of the century was as great as he was."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The given sentence is in a comparative degree, comparing the greatness of the mentioned physiologist to all other physiologists of the century.
 
• To convert it to a positive degree, we need to state that the mentioned physiologist was the greatest of all.
 
• The correct option, Option 4, does this by stating that no other physiologist of the century was as great as he was.
 
• Option 1 is incorrect as it states that all other physiologists were as great as him, which is not the intended meaning of the sentence.
 
• Option 2 is the correct positive degree form, but it is not an exact rephrasing of the given sentence, which makes it less suitable than Option 4.
 
• Option 3 is incorrect as it narrows down the comparison to only the country, while the original sentence compares the mentioned physiologist to all other physiologists of the century.
 
• The correct answer is Option 4.

 

**Correct sentence**: *No other physiologist of the century was as great as he was.*

subject: ENG
question: **Select the option that expresses the following sentence in positive degree of comparison. Istanbul is a beautiful city.**

options.text: The city of Istanbul is as beautiful as other cities.
Istanbul is a very beautiful city.
No other place I have seen is as beautiful as Istanbul.

solution:
The correct answer is: "**No other place I have seen is as beautiful as Istanbul.**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The original sentence "**Istanbul is a beautiful city**" is a positive statement describing the beauty of Istanbul.
 
• To express this in the positive degree of comparison, we use the structure "**more + adjective + than**" when comparing to other places.
 
• Therefore, "*No place I have seen is more beautiful than Istanbul*" conveys the idea that, among the places the speaker has visited, Istanbul is the most beautiful.
 
• This construction emphasizes the positive quality of Istanbul's beauty without making a direct comparison to other places.
 
• The positive degree is achieved by using "**more**" followed by the adjective ("**beautiful**") and "**than**" to indicate the comparison.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 4**.

subject: ENG
question: Select the sentence in the future tense.

options.text: I could be twenty five next Sunday.
I should be twenty five next Sunday.
I have been twenty five next Sunday.
I will be twenty five next Sunday.

solution:
The correct answer is ‘4’ i.e. I will be twenty five next Sunday.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence 'I will be twenty five next Sunday' is in the future tense.
 
 
• The use of **'will be'** indicates an event that is certain to happen in the future.
 
 
 
• The other options are not in the future tense:
 
 
• **Option 1:** 'I could be twenty five next Sunday' uses 'could,' which indicates possibility but not a certain future event.
 
• **Option 2:** 'I should be twenty five next Sunday' uses 'should,' which indicates obligation or expectation, not a certain future event.
 
• **Option 3:** 'I have been twenty five next Sunday' is grammatically incorrect because it mixes present perfect tense with a future time reference.
 
 

 

Hence, the correct answer is option 4.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Future tense in English can be formed using 'will' followed by the base form of the verb.
 
 
• **Example:** *She will arrive tomorrow.*

question:
**Directions: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement.**

Two senior officers have been entrusted with the responsibility __by organize__ the reception of the guest.
solution:
The correct answer is **'of organizing'**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

In the given sentence, the usage of **'by organize'** is incorrect Instead use **'of organizing' 

'Organize' is a verb **that means 'arrange systematically or in order.' 

__
 
• **In the given sentence,****'of'** is used which is a preposition and we know that we have to use **a prepositional object** after the preposition and it can be a **noun/pronoun.**
 
• **The prepositional object **can be a noun/pronoun/gerund, a Gerund is a verb form and if we make a gerund we have to use '**ing' **form after it.
 
• We have to use the preposition **'of' **instead of **'by'** because the former one means **'expressing the relationship between and general category and something which belongs to such category' **while** 'by' **means ‘**as a means of**’ something or someone.
 
• '**By**' preposition often comes in a **passive **sentence.
 
• From the meaning of preposition, we can say that the noun '**responsibility**' will take the preposition '**of**'.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• When '**of**' is used after the noun '**responsibility'**, the definite article must be used before the noun.
 
• Let's see an example
 
 
• The governor-general has the** responsibility of** appointing the members of the Queen’s Privy Council for Canada.
 
 

**So the correct sentence is:** *Two senior officers have been entrusted with the responsibility **of organizing** the reception of the guest.*

Gitanjali __did not had__ school yesterday because it was a second Saturday.
solution:
The correct answer is **"did not have"**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given underlined segment, the use of **the form of the verb** 'had' is **incorrect**.
 
• The verb '**had**' is the **past form** of 'have' and since '**did**' is the **past form** of 'do', **two past forms don't come together in a single sentence**.
 
• **When there is an auxiliary verb (here, did)**, the **main verb (here, had) does not need to be marked for tense**, because **the tense is shown in the auxiliary**.
 
• The verb that follows 'did' should be used in its base form.
 
• Therefore, the **base form of the verb 'had'** i.e. **'have' **should be **used here**.
 
• **Hence**, the correct answer is **option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence__: ***Gitanjali **did not have** school yesterday because it was a second Saturday.*

• However, in a **sentence** about the **past without an auxiliary verb**, the **main verb does need to be in the past tense form**.

The ﬁring of the missile __not only killed innocent persons and also__ created a political furore.

options.text: but killed innocent person and also
not only kill innocent persons and also
not only killed innocent persons but also

solution:
The correct answer is **"​not only killed innocent persons but also"**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the **use of the conjunction 'and'** is **incorrect**.
 
• The **conjunction 'and'** is used **to connect words of the same part of speech, clauses, or sentences, that are to be taken jointly**.
 
• The **conjunction 'but'** is used **to introduce a response expressing a feeling such as surprise or anger**.
 
• The construction "**not only...but (also)**" is called **correlative conjunction**. It is **used to present two related pieces of information**.
 
• **Both pieces of information are being presented as surprising or unexpected**, with the **second one being even more surprising than the first**.
 
• **Hence**, the correct answer is **option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence__: ***The ﬁring of the missile **not only killed innocent persons but also** created a political furore*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• ***Correlative conjunctions** are sort of like tag-team conjunctions. They come in pairs, and you have to use both of them in different places in a sentence to make them work. They get their name from the fact that they work together (co-) and relate one sentence element to another. **Correlative conjunctions** include pairs such as **"both/and", "either/or", "neither/nor", "not/but" and "not only/but also"**.*

• **The past perfect continuous tense **(also known as the past perfect progressive tense) shows that **an action that started in the past continued up until another time in the past.** The past perfect continuous tense is constructed using **had been + the verb’s present participle (root + -ing). **
 
• And we also know that **'before'** used to connect earlier events to the moment of speaking or** to a point of time in the past. **
 
 
• *Example: I introduced Tom to Olivia last night. They hadn’t met before. (up to that point in the past)*

• The structure of Present Perfect Continuous:

 
 
• Subject+has/have+been+v1+ing+object+since/for+time.

• The usage of **before, after and until:**

• If we use '**neither**', then make sure the **sentence does not have any other negatives preceding it**. If we prefer **to use a negative**, then we have to **use** '**either**'.
 
• The **correlative conjunction** "**either/or**" should be used **in place of** "neither/nor".
 
• '**Either/or**' is used in a sentence **in the affirmative sense when referring to a choice between two possibilities**.
 
• '**Either**' is **always paired with** '**or**' and '**neither**' is **always paired with** '**nor**'.

• The relative pronoun 'which' is used for animals in general or non-living things.

 
 
• **Example:** *Raghav** bought the top hybrid car, which will help him save on gas.*
 
 
 
• “Who” is a subjective pronoun and “Whom” is an objective pronoun.
 
• “Who” is always subject to a verb, and “whom” is always working as an object in a sentence. 
 
• If you can replace the word with “he” or "she,” use who.
 
• If you can replace it with “him” or “her,” use whom.
 
• Examples: 
 
 
• *Who would like to go on vacation?*

• ***​*Whose** is a possessive pronoun.
 
• Use it when you're asking (or telling) to whom something belongs.
 
 
• **Example**:* **Whose** chair is this?*
 
 
 
• *​*Therefore, the use of 'which' in the sentence should be replaced with 'who' to make it grammatically correct.
 
• *​​*Correct sentence__: *This is the student **who** won the first prize in the recitation.*

The correct answer is **'invite'**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the usage of 'will invite' is incorrect instead of it use 'invite'
 
• According to grammar, whenever we have a main clause and subordinate clause in the conditional sentence, the usage of will is incorrect in the subordinate clauses hence, we need to omit 'will' from the subordinate clause.
 
• Let's see an example-
 
 
• Unless you call me to say you're not coming, I'll see you at the theatre (= I will see you there if you do not call to say you are not coming).
 
 

**Hence, the correct sentence is-** *He won't come to the party unless **you invite** him personally.*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/9074044cf96dc1d09ca89eac99180c3d7440ade1b364d09d47931959bf693cc8.png] **Confusion Points__***

 
• The word "invited" is in the past tense, and using it in this context would imply that the invitation would have already occurred in the past. However, the sentence is speaking about a future event (the party) and a condition that must be met in the future (the personal invitation).
 
• The verb tenses in the two parts of this conditional sentence need to match. If the first part is in the future tense ("He won't come to the party"), then the second part also needs to be in a tense that refers to future action. The base form of the verb ("invite") is used here to express a condition in the present or future.
 
• If we were talking about a past event, "invited" could be correct. For example: "He didn't come to the party unless you invited him personally."
 
• So, "invite" is the correct option in this context.

The snowstorm will __effect thousand__ of travellers.
solution:
The correct answer is **option 2, "affect thousands."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The verb **"affect"** means** to have an impact on or influence something.**
 
• In this sentence, the snowstorm is having an impact on thousands of travelers.
 
• **"Effect,"** on the other hand, means** to bring about or cause something.**
 
• While the snowstorm may be causing travel disruptions, it is more appropriate to use "**affect**" in this context.
 
• Additionally, "**thousand**" should be pluralized to "**thousands**" to match the subject-verb agreement.
 
• Thus, the correct answer is **Option 2.**

**Therefore, the corrected sentence is**__:* "The snowstorm will __**affect thousands**__ of travelers."*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• The words** "affect"** and **"effect" **are commonly confused due to their similar spellings and pronunciations. However, they have distinct meanings and usage:
 
• **Affect (verb)**: "Affect" is typically used as a verb and relates to influencing, impacting, or producing a change in something. It refers to the action of having an effect on someone or something.
 
 
• Example: "The loud noise affected my concentration, making it difficult to focus."
 
 
 
• **Effect (noun or verb)**: "Effect" can be used as both a noun and a verb, and it generally refers to the result, outcome, or consequence of an action or event.
 
• **As a noun:**
 
 
• Example: "The new policies had a positive effect on employee morale."
 
 
 
• **As a verb:**
 
 
• Example: "The company aimed to effect changes in its organizational structure."
 
 
 
• To summarize, "**affect**" is a verb used to describe the act of influencing or impacting something, while "**effect**" is a noun (or verb) that represents the result or consequence of an action.

Dad said that, "__She would have been a great sister if she was just a bit more careful__".

options.text: that, "She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful"
"She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful"
"She would have been a greatest sister if she was just a bit more careful"

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• This is because, in English grammar, **when referring to hypothetical situations or conditions** that are contrary to fact, **we often use "were"** **instead** of** "was" **after "if" even when the subject is singular.
 
• This is a usage pattern known as the subjunctive mood.
 
• So,* "if she were just a bit more careful"* is **more grammatically correct than** *"if she was just a bit more careful".*
 
• Also, we use** 'that'** to **introduce reported speech** when the words are not the speaker’s exact words (i.e., when the speaker is paraphrasing, summarizing, or interpreting the original speaker’s words). So,** 'Dad said that' **is *appropriate here.*

Therefore, the **correct sentence** is:* "Dad said that, 'She would have been a great sister if she were just a bit more careful'".*

Thus,** option 2** is the correct answer.

question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.**

The new restaurant is __more better__ than the old one.
solution:
The correct answer is: **Better**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The use of "more" before "better" is incorrect as "**better**" is already a comparative form of the adjective "**good**".
 
• The correct comparative form of "**good**" is "**better**", and the superlative form is "**the best**".
 
• Therefore, the correct sentence should be "*The new restaurant is better than the old one.*"

Hence, **option 2** is the correct answer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The comparative and superlative forms of adjectives are used to compare and describe different degrees of a particular quality.
 
• 
 
**Comparative Form**:

 
 
• 
 
**Usage**: The comparative form is used when you are comparing two things or two groups.

 
 
• 
 
**Formation**: Most adjectives form the comparative by adding "-er" (e.g., faster, taller) or by using "more" before the adjective (e.g., more beautiful, more interesting).

 
 
• 
 
**Example**: The cat is faster than the dog.

 
 
 
 
• 
 
**Superlative Form**:

 
 
• 
 
**Usage**: The superlative form is used when you are comparing more than two things or groups, indicating the highest degree of quality.

 
 
• 
 
**Formation**: Most adjectives form the superlative by adding "-est" (e.g., fastest, tallest) or by using "most" before the adjective (e.g., most beautiful, most interesting).

 
 
• 
 
**Example**: The cheetah is the fastest land animal.

question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

Can you please tell me __where__ __is the city park ?__
solution:
The correct answer is: "**where the city park is?**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The overall structure of the sentence is an **interrogative sentence**, starting with the auxiliary verb **"can"**.
 
• It's asking someone else to provide information. An embedded indirect question "where the city park is" is used, and this follows English rule of structure for indirect questions.
 
• In indirect questions or embedded questions, the usual word order of a statement is kept. That's why we use "where the city park is" instead of "where is the city park?" which is how the question would be posed directly.
 
• The **subject** (the city park) precedes the** auxiliary verb** (is) in indirect questions, hence 'where the city park is' is correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is: ***Can you please tell me where the city park is ?***

Select the option that corrects the following sentence.

He has broken his leg yesterday.

options.text: He has broke his leg yesterday.
He have broken his leg yesterday.
He had broke his leg yesterday.

solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e., He broke his leg yesterday.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence "He has broken his leg yesterday" is incorrect due to the use of the present perfect tense with a specific past time reference (**'yesterday'**).
 
• The correct way to refer to a specific time in the past (**'yesterday'**) is by using the **simple past tense**.
 
• Therefore, we should say "He broke his leg yesterday.".

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Correct sentence: *He broke his leg yesterday.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The present perfect tense (has/have + past participle) is used to describe actions that have occurred at an unspecified time before now, not specific past times like 'yesterday'.
 
 
• **Example**: He has broken his leg. (unspecified time)
 
 
 
• Simple past is used for actions completed at a specific time in the past.
 
 
• **Example**: He broke his leg last week. (specific time)

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.

Rimjhim received __a children’s very illustrated colourful atlas__ on her 10th birthday.

options.text: a very illustrated colourful atlas children
a colourful very illustrated children’s atla
a very colourful illustrated children’s atlas
an very illustrated colourful children’s atlas

solution:
The correct answer is '3' i.e., a very colourful illustrated children’s atlas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence "Rimjhim received a children’s very illustrated colourful atlas on her 10th birthday" is incorrect due to the improper order of adjectives.
 
• The order of adjectives in English typically follows this sequence: quantity, quality, size, age, shape, color, proper adjective (often nationality, other place of origin, or material), and purpose or qualifier.
 
• Accordingly, "very" (emphasizer) should come first, then "colourful" (quality), and finally "illustrated" (participle acting as an adjective).
 
• Therefore, the phrase should be "a very colourful illustrated children’s atlas."

Hence, the correct answer is option 3.

Correct sentence: *Rimjhim received a very colourful illustrated children’s atlas on her 10th birthday.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The rules for the correct order of adjectives ensure clear and natural-sounding descriptions in English.
 
 
• **Example**: She bought a beautiful large old round wooden table.
 
 
 
• This sequence helps in maintaining a logical and readable structure in sentences that include multiple adjectives.

Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.

I was looking for a __barren seat__ in the bus but could not find one.
solution:
The correct answer is: **Option 2** i.e. **vacant seat**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"barren"** means something that is unproductive, empty, or lacking vegetation. • **Example: **The farmer struggled with the barren land that yielded no crops.
 
 
 
• **"Vacant" **refers to something that is not occupied or filled; available for use. • **Example: **I found a vacant seat at the back of the bus.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that "vacant seat" is the correct term to use instead of "barren seat".

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 2** i.e. **vacant seat**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Deserted seat **: A seat that is abandoned or left empty by people.

 
 
• **Example:** The deserted seat in the park looked lonely.
 
 
 
• **Hollow seat **: A seat that is empty inside or has a space within.
 
 
• **Example: **The hollow seat was not very comfortable to sit on.

• It logically orders the sentence, making it easy to understand that she finished eating her breakfast in a quick manner.
 
• The structure adheres to standard English.
 
 
• **syntax: subject + verb + object + adverb.**
 
 
 
• Placing** "quickly"** after **"breakfast"** avoids **misplaced modifiers and ensures that "quickly" modifies how she finished her breakfast.**
 
• This construction provides a** natural, fluent reading experience, enhancing readability.**

• **"Quickly her breakfast finished" **is awkward and does not follow standard English syntax; it also implies the breakfast is finishing itself.
 
• **"Finished breakfast hers quickly"** is ungrammatical and incorrectly orders the possessive pronoun and breakfast.

subject: ENG
question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.

I quietly went out __at__ the door into the veranda.
solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary issue in the sentence is the use of an** incorrect preposition.**
 
• The phrase "at the door" is not appropriate in this context.
 
• The correct phrase should be **"through the door,"** which indicates the action of passing from one side of the door to the other.
 
• Thus, "through" is the most appropriate substitution for the underlined segment.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"I quietly went out** through the door** into the veranda."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **No substitution required** would be the correct option if the original sentence was already correct, but "at the door" is incorrect in this context.
 
• **From** could indicate direction but does not fit well here.
 
• **By** indicates proximity but not the action of moving through a door.

• The phrase **"prefer eating at home from eating out" **is** incorrect.**

• Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"**Well, I prefer eating at home to eating out."***

• **Option 4:** "while eating out" is incorrect as it changes the meaning of the sentence.

My brother works for **__a MNC.__**
solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The article **'an'** is used before words that begin with a vowel sound.
 
• In the sentence *"My brother works for a MNC,"* the highlighted part uses the article **'a'**, which is incorrect because the abbreviation **'MNC'** begins with a vowel sound ('em').
 
• The correct article to use is **'an'**, resulting in **'an MNC.'**

Correct sentence: *My brother works for an MNC.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Articles:**
 
 
• **'a'** is used before words that begin with a consonant sound, e.g., "a book."
 
• **'an'** is used before words that begin with a vowel sound, e.g., "an apple."
 
• The choice of article depends on the sound of the word following it, not necessarily the spelling.
 
 
 
• **Abbreviations:**
 
 
• When abbreviations begin with a vowel sound, the article **'an'** is used, e.g., "an MBA."
 
• When abbreviations begin with a consonant sound, the article **'a'** is used, e.g., "a CEO."
 
 
</ul

• Structure: Subject + is/are + verb-ing.
 
• Example: She **is reading** a book.

Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

It is difficult to diagnose malaria because its first symptoms __**are similar to any viral fever.**__

options.text: are similar to those of an any viral fever
is similar to those of any other viral fever
is similar to those of any viral fevers

solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. are similar to those of any viral fever.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence highlights a comparison between the initial symptoms of malaria and the symptoms of a viral fever. To ensure grammatical accuracy and clarity, the comparison must be correctly structured.
 
• The phrase **"those of"** is used to refer back to the symptoms mentioned earlier in the sentence, avoiding redundancy.
 
• The correct option, **"are similar to those of any viral fever,"** ensures proper comparison by matching the plural subject **"symptoms"** with the plural verb **"are."**

Correct sentence: *It is difficult to diagnose malaria because its first symptoms **are similar to those of any viral fever**.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Why other options are incorrect:**
 
 
• **Option 1: "are similar to all fevers" -** This is overly broad and incorrect, as the sentence specifically compares malaria symptoms to viral fevers, not all fevers.
 
• **Option 3: "is similar to those of any other viral fever" -** The use of "is" is incorrect as the subject "symptoms" is plural.
 
• **Option 4: "is similar to those of any viral fevers" -** The plural "fevers" is unnecessary and ungrammatical in this context.
 
 
 
• **Key Grammar Rule:** Ensure subject-verb agreement and maintain logical clarity when making comparisons.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

This is __the most toughest exam __that I have ever taken.
solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. the toughest exam .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"most"** is used to form the superlative degree of adjectives, but it cannot be paired with an adjective that is already in its superlative form, such as **"toughest."**
 
• The correct form is simply **"the toughest exam"** without the word **"most."**
 
• Using **"most toughest"** is redundant and grammatically incorrect.

Correct sentence: *This is the toughest exam that I have ever taken.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Superlative Degree:**

 
 
• **Definition:** Used to compare three or more things, showing the highest degree of the quality being described.
 
• **Example:** "This is the tallest building in the city."
 
• **Rule:** Do not use "most" with adjectives that already have superlative forms ending in "-est" (e.g., tallest, smartest, toughest).
 
 
 
• **Common Errors:**
 
 
• Redundancy: Using both "most" and the "-est" form together (e.g., "most fastest").
 
• Incorrect pairing of comparative and superlative forms.
 
 
</ul

• **Less:** Used with uncountable nouns to indicate a smaller amount (e.g., "less water").
 
• **Little:** Used with uncountable nouns to indicate a small amount (e.g., "little time").
 
• **Fewer:** Used with plural countable nouns to compare two quantities (e.g., "fewer books").

subject: ENG
question: Identify the correct formula to find the potential difference between two points.
solution:
The correct answer is **V=W/Q**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• The electric potential difference is the difference in electric potential (V) between the final and the initial location when work is done upon a charge to change its potential energy.
 
• The potential difference between two points is equal to the work done in moving a unit of positive charge from one point to the other.
 
 
• **V = W/Q (V = potential difference, W = work done, Q = charge)**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The electric potential difference between two points in an electric circuit carrying some current is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to another.
 
• Thus, a potential difference is the work done per unit charge and is given as V =W/Q.

subject: ENG
question:
**Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.**

You are __so efficient as he__
solution:
The correct answer is: **as efficient as he is**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence "You are as efficient as he is." is a grammatically correct comparative sentence, and its correctness can be explained based on comparative structures, subject pronouns, and parallelism in sentence construction.
 
• Comparative Structure Using "as...as"
 
 
• In English grammar, when making comparisons of equality, we use the structure:
 
• **as + adjective/adverb + as + noun/pronoun**
 
 
 
• In this case, the **adjective** "efficient" is used to compare the efficiency of **"you" **and **"he."**
 
• Example:
 
 
• "You are as charming as he is."
 
 
 
• The Role of **"he"** as a **Subject Pronoun**
 
 
• Here, "he" is a subject pronoun that refers to the full clause "he is efficient."
 
 
 
• The Role of **"is" **in **Parallel Structure**
 
 
• To maintain parallelism, the second part of the sentence should mirror the first part. The verb** "is" **is necessary to complete the comparison clearly.
 
• "You are as efficient as he is (efficient)."
 
 

​Hence, the correct answer is: **as efficient as he is**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Why not "him" in place of 'he'?**

 
 
• **​**A common mistake in informal English is using an object pronoun like "him" instead of a subject pronoun "he."
 
• **Incorrect:** "You are as efficient as him."
 
• **Correct: **"You are as efficient as he is."
 
 
 
• **Rule: Subject Pronoun Use**
 
 
• According to standard grammar rules, when making a comparison where the second clause is implied, the** subject pronoun** must be used because it functions as the subject of an understood verb.

• **Example:** *She had been completing her homework. *

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indirect Speech:** The old woman told the children that they should always be kind to animals and that she had been doing so her entire life.
 
• **Key Conversions (Indirect to Direct):**
 
 
• **"told the children" becomes "said to the children"**
 
 
• When converting back to direct speech, the reporting verb "told" followed by an object ("the children") changes back to **"said to."**
 
 
 
• **"they should" becomes "You should"**
 
 
• The third-person pronoun "they" reverts to the second-person pronoun **"You"** since the old woman is addressing the children directly. The modal verb "should" typically remains **"should"** in direct speech.
 
 
 
• **"she had been doing" becomes "I have been doing"**
 
 
• The **Past Perfect Continuous** tense ("had been doing") changes back to the **Present Perfect Continuous** tense ("have been doing") in direct speech.
 
 
 
• **"her" becomes "my"**
 
 
• The third-person possessive pronoun "her" reverts to the first-person **"my."**
 
 
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *The old woman said to the children, "You should always be kind to animals, and I have been doing so my entire life."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** "...I have done so my entire life." 

 
 
• Incorrect because "have done" (Present Perfect) would change to "had done" (Past Perfect) in indirect speech, not the required "had been doing" (Past Perfect Continuous).
 
 
 
• **Option 3:** "...and I had been doing so my entire life." 
 
 
• While grammatically possible in some contexts, backshifting usually means the direct speech was in the present perfect continuous. Using past perfect continuous in direct speech here alters the immediacy of her ongoing action.
 
 
 
• **Option 4:** "...You must always be kind..." 
 
 
• Incorrect because the modal "must" generally changes to "had to" in indirect speech, whereas "should" remains "should."

• **Option 1:** Incorrect because it keeps the present perfect tense ("has completed") instead of back-shifting to the past perfect.
 
• **Option 3:** Incorrect because it fails to change the first-person pronouns ("I" and "my"), which changes the meaning of who completed the task.
 
• **Option 4:** Incorrect because it fails to change the pronoun "I" and the tense "have completed."

subject: ENG
question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct voice.

The historian concluded that the ancient civilization had developed advanced irrigation techniques long before its demise.

options.text: The historian said, "The ancient civilization had developed advanced irrigation techniques long before its demise."
The historian said, "The ancient civilization developed advanced irrigation techniques long before its demise."
The historian concluded, "The ancient civilization develops advanced irrigation techniques."
The historian said, "The ancient civilization has developed advanced irrigation techniques."

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indirect Speech:** The historian concluded that the ancient civilization had developed advanced irrigation techniques long before its demise.
 
• **Tense Change (Indirect to Direct):** In indirect speech, the **Past Perfect** tense ("had developed") is used to report an action that was already in the **Simple Past** ("developed") in the original direct speech. When converting back to direct voice, we shift the tense forward.
 
• **Reporting Verb:** The reporting verb **"concluded"** in indirect speech can be represented by **"said"** in direct speech while maintaining the core meaning.
 
• **Conjunction:** The conjunction **"that"** is removed, and the original statement is placed within quotation marks.
 
• **Context:** Since the historian is talking about a completed historical event, the **Simple Past** ("developed") is the most natural and grammatically correct form for the original statement.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The historian said, 'The ancient civilization developed advanced irrigation techniques long before its demise.'"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** Incorrect because it retains **"had developed"** (Past Perfect). While technically possible for very specific sequences of past events, "had developed" in indirect speech is almost always a backshifted "developed" (Simple Past) from the direct version.
 
• **Option 3:** Incorrect because it uses **"develops"** (Simple Present), which suggests a habitual action or a current state, which does not fit a historical demise.
 
• **Option 4:** Incorrect because it uses **"has developed"** (Present Perfect), which implies a connection to the present that is inconsistent with a civilization that has already met its demise.

__
 
• **Indirect Speech:** The scientist told the students that light travels faster than sound.
 
• **Universal Truth Rule:** If the reported speech expresses a **universal truth, scientific fact, or habitual action**, the tense of the verb remains unchanged even if the reporting verb is in the past tense. Since "light travels faster than sound" is a scientific fact, the present tense is retained in both direct and indirect speech.
 
• **Reporting Verb (Indirect to Direct):** The verb **"told"** (followed by an object "the students") typically converts back to **"said to"** in direct speech.
 
• **Punctuation:** In direct speech, the conjunction "that" is removed, a comma is placed after the reporting clause, and the spoken words are enclosed in quotation marks starting with a capital letter.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The scientist said to the students, 'Light travels faster than sound.'"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Option 3:** Incorrect because it uses **"is traveling"** (Present Continuous), which suggests a specific instance of travel rather than a general scientific property.
 
• **Option 4:** Incorrect because it uses **"will travel"** (Future Simple), which implies the fact only applies to the future.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• To convert **Indirect Speech** to **Direct Speech**, we must reverse the tense back-shifting that occurred during reporting.
 
• The modal **"could"** in indirect speech generally shifts back to **"can"** in direct speech to maintain the original perspective of the speaker.
 
• The past perfect continuous tense **"had been recording"** in indirect speech typically originates from the present perfect continuous **"have been recording"** in direct speech.
 
• Pronouns also shift: the third-person **"he"** (referring to the suspect) must be changed to the second-person **"you"** as the detective is addressing the suspect directly.

Correct sentence: *The detective asked the suspect, "How **can you have committed** the crime without leaving any evidence when the security cameras **have been recording** all night?"*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Direct to Indirect Tense Shifting:**

 
 
• **Present Perfect Continuous** (have been recording) becomes **Past Perfect Continuous** (had been recording).
 
• **Can** becomes **Could**.
 
• **Present Perfect** (have committed) becomes **Past Perfect** (had committed/could have committed in modal context).
 
 
 
• **Reporting Interrogative Sentences:**
 
 
• In "Wh-" questions, the question word (how, what, where) acts as the connector.
 
• The sentence structure changes from **interrogative** (Verb + Subject) in direct speech to **assertive** (Subject + Verb) in indirect speech.

• When converting direct speech into indirect speech for past tense sentences, the tense of the verbs typically changes to the past perfect or past perfect continuous.
 
• "I finished my project" changes to "he had finished his project" in indirect speech because the past simple tense becomes past perfect tense.
 
• "I was working on a new one" changes to "he had been working on a new one" in indirect speech because the past continuous tense becomes past perfect continuous tense.

Correct sentence: *He said that he had finished his project and he had been working on a new one.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• In indirect speech, the pronouns and verbs are adjusted to reflect the perspective of the speaker. For example, "I" becomes "he" or "she" depending on the subject.
 
• Time expressions such as "today," "yesterday," or "tomorrow" may also change. However, in this case, there are no time expressions in the original sentence.
 
• Option 1 is incorrect because "he was working" is not the appropriate conversion for the past continuous tense in indirect speech.
 
• Option 3 is incorrect because "he finished his project" does not reflect the proper change to past perfect tense.
 
• Option 4 is incorrect because "he had been finishing his project" implies an ongoing action, which is not conveyed in the original sentence.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect voice.

The director said, "The new actor will be arriving shortly."

options.text: The director said that the new actor would be arriving shortly.
The director said that the new actor will be arriving shortly.
The director said that the new actor would arrive shortly.
The director said that the new actor had been arriving shortly.

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Direct Speech:** The director said, "The new actor will be arriving shortly."
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• **Modal Verb Change (Backshifting):**
 
 
• When the reporting verb is in the past ("said"), modal verbs in the direct speech must shift to their past forms.
 
• The modal **"will"** changes to **"would."**
 
 
 
• **Tense Maintenance (Continuous Aspect):**
 
 
• The original sentence is in the Future Continuous ("will be arriving").
 
• In indirect speech, the continuous aspect **"be arriving"** is preserved after the shifted modal **"would."**
 
 
 
• **Conjunction:**
 
 
• The comma and quotation marks are removed and replaced by **"that"** to connect the reporting clause with the reported statement.
 
 
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The director said that the new actor would be arriving shortly."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2:** Fails to shift the modal "will" to "would," which is necessary when the reporting verb is in the past.
 
• **Option 3:** Changes the aspect from continuous ("be arriving") to simple ("arrive"), which alters the original meaning of the speaker.
 
• **Option 4:** Uses the past perfect continuous ("had been arriving"), which incorrectly implies a past habitual action rather than a future planned arrival.

subject: ENG
question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

Fiona enquired whether I had gone to school on Tuesday

options.text: “Had you been going to school on Tuesday?” Fiona asked me.
“Where are you going on Tuesday?’’ Fiona asked me.
“Did you go to school on Tuesday?’’ Fiona asked me.
“Are you gone to school on Tuesday? Fiona enquired.

solution:
The correct answer is **“Did you go to school on Tuesday?’’ Fiona asked me****.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is enquiring about something. So, the Direct Speech of this sentence must be an interrogative sentence.
 
• The rule of changing an indirect speech into a direct speech of an Interrogative sentence is as follows:
 
 
• In Indirect Narration, interrogative Verbs such as **“ask”, “enquire”, “demand”, “want to know”** etc are used as Reporting Verbs before the Reported Speech in place of simple Verb **“say” or “tell”**.
 
• **E.g.**__- He said to me, "Are you ill?" **(Direct Speech)**
 
• He **asked** (or **enquired of**) me if (or whether) I was ill. **(Indirect Speech)**
 
• If the Reported Speech in Direct Narration is introduced by Verbs like **“ be”, “have”, “do”, or any other auxiliary Verbs like “can”, “shall”, “will”**, the connective **“ if ”, “ whether ”** is used after the Reporting Verb or object of the Reporting verb in the Indirect Narration.
 
• __**E.g.**__- He said to me, "Are you ill?" **(Direct Speech)**
 
• He asked (or enquired of) me **if** (or **whether**) I was ill. **(Indirect Speech)**** **
 
 

 Hence, the correct answer is **“Did you go to school on Tuesday?’’ Fiona asked me.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **What is Direct & Indirect Speech?**

 
 
• **Direct speech** – reporting the message of the speaker in the exact words as spoken by him.
 
• **Direct speech example:** Maya said, "I am busy now."
 
• **Indirect speech **– reporting the message of the speaker in our own words.
 
• **Indirect speech example:** Maya said that she was busy then.

subject: ENG
question:
Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement from the given alternatives:

Sujit said, "Can you pass me the chilli sauce please?"

options.text: Sujit requested if he could pass him the chilli sauce please.
Sujit requested if he can pass him the chilli sauce please.
Sujit requested if he can pass him the chilli sauce.
Sujit requested if he could pass him the chilli sauce.

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Direct Speech:** Sujit said, "Can you pass me the chilli sauce please?"
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• **Reporting verb:**
 
 
• The word "please" indicates a request. Therefore, the reporting verb **"said"** is converted to **"requested"**.
 
 
 
• **"Can" becomes "could":**
 
 
• When the reporting verb is in the past tense ("said/requested"), the modal verb **"can"** must be changed to its past form **"could"** in indirect speech.
 
 
 
• **Pronoun change:**
 
 
• The first-person pronoun **"me"** refers to the speaker (Sujit), so it changes to the third-person **"him"**.
 
 
 
• **Removal of "Please":**
 
 
• In indirect speech, the word **"please"** is omitted because the sense of requesting is already conveyed by the reporting verb "requested."
 
 
 
 
 
• **Structure:** Since the direct speech is a Yes/No question, we use the conjunction **"if"** or **"whether"** to join the reporting clause and the reported speech.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Sujit requested if he could pass him the chilli sauce."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** "Sujit requested if he could pass him the chilli sauce please." 

 
 
• Incorrect because it redundantly includes the word "please" at the end.
 
 
 
• **Option 2:** "Sujit requested if he can pass him the chilli sauce please." 
 
 
• Incorrect because "can" is not changed to "could" and it retains "please."
 
 
 
• **Option 3:** "Sujit requested if he can pass him the chilli sauce." 
 
 
• Incorrect because the modal verb "can" remains in the present tense, which does not match the past tense reporting verb.

• **Key Conversions:**

__
 
• **Reporting Verb:** The presence of the word **"please"** in the direct speech indicates a request. Therefore, the reporting verb "said" is changed to **"requested"**.
 
• **Conjunction:** For "Yes/No" questions (questions starting with auxiliary verbs like 'Will'), we use **"if"** or **"whether"** as the conjunction.
 
• **Sentence Structure:** In indirect speech, the interrogative form (verb + subject) changes to the assertive form (subject + verb). Thus, "Will you" becomes **"they would"** (assuming "you" refers to a group).
 
• **Tense Change:** The future modal **"will"** changes to its past form **"would"** because the reporting verb is in the past tense.
 
• **Pronoun Change:** The first-person possessive **"my"** (referring to the manager) changes to the third-person **"his"**.
 
• **Omission:** The word "please" is removed because the verb "requested" already conveys the polite tone.

• **Option 3:** Incorrect because **"would"** must be followed by the base form of the verb (**"attend"**), not the past form ("attended").

**Directions: Given below are four jumbled sentences. Out of the given options pick the one that gives their correct order.**

**A:** According to the EPR, the corporation expects such manufacturers to develop a collect back system for plastic waste.

**B:** The Municipal Corporation has introduced the extended producer's responsibility (EPR) for producers and generators of plastic waste.

**C: **The producers are persons engaged in the manufacture, or import of carrying bags, multilayered packaging and sheets, and persons using them.

• The noun "manufacturers" mentioned in the sentence 'A' refers back to the phrase "**persons engaged in the manufacture**" in the sentence 'C'. Hence, 'A' follows 'C'.
 
• The sentence 'D' is the concluding sentence. Hence, the sentence 'D' is the last sentence.

 

After rearranging the sentences__: *The Municipal Corporation has introduced the extended producer's responsibility (EPR) for producers and generators of plastic waste. question:
**Directions: Given below are four jumbled sentences. Select the option that gives their correct order.**

A. This test is conducted on the fully automated Driving Test Track designed by Maruti Suzuki.

B. Each of these specific skills is to be tested and need to be completed successfully in under seven minutes by the candidate.

C. It is a fully-automated track having six segments to test specific driving skills.

D. The Regional Transport Offices of Delhi have recently introduced a new driving test.
solution:
The correct answer is **"DACB"**.

​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence 'D' is independent of any other sentences as it is giving general information about "**The Regional Transport Offices of Delhi**". Hence, 'D' is the first part.
 
• The phrase "This **test**" in the sentence 'A' refers back to the '**new driving test**' mentioned in the sentence 'D'. Hence, 'A' follows 'D'.
 
• The pronoun 'It' in the sentence 'C' refers back to the '**Driving Test Track**' mentioned in the sentence 'A'. Hence, 'C' follows 'A'.
 
• The phrase "**these specific skills**" in the sentence 'B' refers back to the '**specific driving skills**' mentioned in the sentence 'C'. Hence, 'B' follows 'C'.

 

After rearranging the sentences__: *The Regional Transport Offices of Delhi have recently introduced a new driving test. This test is conducted on the fully automated Driving Test Track designed by Maruti Suzuki. It is a fully-automated track having six segments to test specific driving skills. Each of these specific skills is to be tested and need to be completed successfully in under seven minutes by the candidate.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **__Important Points__**

__
 
• Important Rules to Solve the Para Jumbles__:

 
 
• Read the sentences attentively and try to comprehend the idea or theme of the sentence and eliminate the irrelevant options.
 
• Try to identify the opening (independent sentence) and closing sentences (concluding sentence).
 
• Try to identify the mandatory pairs. Two sentences can be connected through various connectors and other determinants.

question:
**Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the right order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.**

A. That magic is believing in yourself a hundred per cent.

B. There is only one magic in life that can help you turn your dreams into reality.

C. You will be able to face life’s challenges with courage only if you believe in yourself and in your capacity to meet those challenges.

D. Therefore, the most important lesson that a family can teach its members is to have this faith in oneself.
solution:
The correct answer is- 'BACD.' [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• By reading the above-given para we can understand that the paragraph is about *the magic of having faith in one's self*.
 
• Part **B **will come **first**, as it **introduces **the **theme **of the passage (*Magic of belief*).
 
• Part **A **will come **next**, as the **conjunction '***that*' joins the two sentences and provides **more information **about the **subject **(*Magic*).
 
• Part **C **will follow** next**, as it **adds **more **information **about the magic of belief.
 
• Part **D **will **conclude **the passage.
 
• Thus *option 2 *is the correct answer.

The correct sequence is: 

B. There is only one magic in life that can help you turn your dreams into reality.

A. That magic is believing in yourself a hundred per cent.

C. You will be able to face life’s challenges with courage only if you believe in yourself and in your capacity to meet those challenges.

D. Therefore, the most important lesson that a family can teach its members is to have this faith in oneself.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** 

 
• Here are some tips to solve the para jumbles:
 
 
• You need to understand the idea behind the paragraph. If you can understand the idea/theme of the paragraph it is easy to put the sentences in order then.
 
• You should look out for the starting or the concluding sentences in the question. Sometimes they are clearly visible and can help you immensely in identifying the correct sequence.
 
• You need to know the relationships between different sentences to put them in the right sequence. 
 
• You should first fix the relationships of sentences, put them in order and then check the options.
 
• Transition words and contrasting words also help in finding clean relationships between sentences of the sentence rearrangement.
 
• Do not over depend on options, they only confuse you if you keep looking at them, use them as facilitators only, especially to fix your first sentence.
 
• The whole paragraph should have a coherent idea and flow when arranged in the correct order.

question:
**Given below are four jumbled sentences. Out of the given options pick the one that gives their correct order.**

A. The town of Lustenau in Austria claims to have built a world record-breaking bonfire.

B. The structure took three months to build but collapsed in less than half an hour last Saturday evening.

C. Embers from the big fire fell onto nearby market traders, but local fire crews were on hand to make sure that everyone was safe.

D. According to the organizers, the pyre reached as high as 60 meters.
solution:
The correct answer is **'ADBC'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given question is an example of a Para Jumble.
 
• We know that the first statement of a **para jumbled** question is usually an independent general statement, a noun, a universal fact, starting of an incident, or it starts with 'most' or 'once'. 
 
• **Sentence A** will be the starting line because it contains the main idea of the para jumble i.e.the town of Lustenau that built a world record-breaking bonfire.
 
• However, **Sentence D** states that the pyre reached as high as 60 meters. So, **D** will follow **A**.
 
• Let's look at the meaning of Pyre:-
 
 
• **Pyre **- a heap of combustible material, especially one for burning a corpse as part of a funeral ceremony.
 
 
 
• Further,** Sentence B** states that the structure took three months to build but collapsed in less than half an hour & **Sentence C** states that Embers from the big fire fell onto nearby market traders. So, **C** will follow **B**.
 
• Let's look at the meaning of Embers:-
 
 
• **Embers **- a small piece of burning or glowing coal or wood in a dying fire.
 
 
 
• Thus, the correct sequence:
 
 
• **A**. The town of Lustenau in Austria claims to have built a world record-breaking bonfire.
 
• **D**. According to the organizers, the pyre reached as high as 60 meters.
 
• **B**. The structure took three months to build but collapsed in less than half an hour last Saturday evening.
 
• **C**. Embers from the big fire fell onto nearby market traders, but local fire crews were on hand to make sure that everyone was safe.

 
 
 

**Correct Sequence:__** *The town of Lustenau in Austria claims to have built a world record-breaking bonfire. According to the organizers, the pyre reached as high as 60 meters. The structure took three months to build but collapsed in less than half an hour last Saturday evening. Embers from the big fire fell onto nearby market traders, but local fire crews were on hand to make sure that everyone was safe.*

• We know that the first statement of a sentence jumbled question is usually an independent general statement, a noun, a universal fact, starting of an incident, or it starts with 'most' or 'once'.

subject: ENG
question:
**Given below are four sentences in jumbled order. Select the option that gives their correct order.**

A. He seemed to remain that high for nearly two years.

B. Kari, the elephant was five months old when he was given to me to take care of.

C. We grew together, that is probably why I never found out just how tall he was.

D. I was nine years old and I could reach his back if I stood on tiptoe.
solution:
The correct answer is '**BDAC**'.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given question is an example of a Para Jumble.
 
• We know that the first statement of a para jumbled question is usually an independent general statement, a noun, a universal fact, starting off a story, starting of an incident or an event, or it starts with 'most' or 'once'.
 
• **Sentence B** will be the starting line because it contains the main idea of the para jumble i.e. Kari, the elephant.
 
• However, **Sentence D** states that the narrator was nine years old when the elephant was given to him to take care of. He could reach his back if he stood on tiptoe.
 
• So, **D** will follow **B**.
 
• **Sentence A **will be next because it mentions **'that high'** which corresponds to the height of the elephant mentioned in **sentence D.**
 
• So, **C** will follow **A **because it tells why the narrator never found out how tall Kari was.
 
• Thus, the correct sequence is:
 
 
• **B**: Kari, the elephant was five months old when he was given to me to take care of.
 
• **D**: I was nine years old and I could reach his back if I stood on tiptoe.
 
• **A**: He seemed to remain that high for nearly two years.
 
• **C**: We grew together, that is probably why I never found out just how tall he was.

 
 
 

**Correct Sequence:__** *Kari, the elephant was five months old when he was given to me to take care of. I was nine years old and I could reach his back if I stood on tiptoe. He seemed to remain that high for nearly two years. We grew together, that is probably why I never found out just how tall he was.*

D. Which the traditional society of India tolerates
solution:
The correct answer is **"C, A, D, B."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• C. It has frequently been claimed: This sentence introduces the claim or thesis, so it serves as the leading statement or introduction. It informs the reader that an assertion is about to be discussed which has been made multiple times before.
 
• A. That the only true individual: This phrase extends the claim mentioned in paragraph "C." It tells us the subject of this claim is a particular type of person categorized as the 'true individual,' but does not specify yet who this individual is.
 
• D. Whom the traditional society of India tolerates: This part of the sentence is specifying who this 'true individual' is. It suggests that this individual is someone who is tolerated by traditional society in India. At this point, the reader knows the claim is about a particular type of individual who is acceptable in traditional Indian society.
 
• B. Is the holy man: The final phrase, "Is the holy man," serves as the conclusion of the argument. It identifies and clarifies who this 'true individual' is. It finalizes the claim by stating that this 'true individual,' tolerated by traditional Indian society, is a holy man.
 
 
 
• This ordering provides a complete, coherent thought and is chronologically correct because it starts by stating the claim, identifies the topic, gives a further attribute to this topic regarding its acceptance in traditional Indian society, and ends by identifying who exactly this 'true individual' is - a holy man.

**Correct sentence**: *It has frequently been claimed (C) that the only true individual (A) which the traditional society of India tolerates (D) **is the holy man (B) **.*

• **Sentence P is the first sentence** because it introduces the subject (the old man) and establishes his physical presence and mood:
 
 
• "The old man, with his kind eyes and twisted hands, smiled softly."
 
 
 
• **Sentence Q follows** to provide context and background for the man, explaining his profession and the setting of the scene:
 
 
• "He had lived a whole life as a woodcarver, and his store was a museum of fragile works of art."
 
 
 
• **Sentence R is the third sentence** as it transitions from the general store to the specific piece he is working on at this moment:

• The correct sequence is **PQRS**.

solution:
The correct answer is '**CBAD**'.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given question is an example of a Para Jumble.

• Sentence C will be the first statement because it is a general independent statement and it is talking about the common problem of **pollution**.
 
• Sentence B will be the next sentence as it further tells us about the time this problem is prevalent. 
 
• Sentence A will be the next sentence because it is telling us about the current situation of pollution.
 
• Lastly, Sentence D will be used.
 
• Thus, the sequence becomes:
 
 
• C: Pollution has become a very common yet serious issue in today’s world.
 
• B: It has been there in different forms since a long time, even before human evolution, such as volcanic eruptions, wildfire which led to various photochemical reactions in the atmosphere.
 
• A: The current concern is that it is rising day by day due to various resources of pollutants.
 
• D: And, one of the main pollutants are humans and man-made machines.

• The passage describes the air as "**thick**" with the smell of paper and dust. When a sensation is described as thick or dense, it often suggests it is **overwhelming**.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.

If a product placement

P. we are either less likely to notice the placement

Q. our attention is fixated on what will happen next,

R. or more likely to be annoyed by it if we do notice it

S. appears at the climax, the moment when
solution:
The correct order of the parts of the sentence is: SQPR

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **S. appears at the climax, the moment when**
 
• This sentence sets the context by stating that a product placement occurs at the climax, which is the moment of highest intensity or suspense in a narrative.
 
• **Q. our attention is fixated on what will happen next,**
 
• The sentence starting with "our attention is fixated" describes the state of focus or concentration that occurs during the climax. At this point, the audience is eagerly anticipating what will happen next in the story.
 
• **P. we are either less likely to notice the placement**
 
• This statement suggests that due to the heightened focus on the narrative's unfolding events, there is a reduced likelihood of noticing the product placement. The audience's attention is primarily directed towards the storyline rather than the presence of any advertising.
 
• **R. or more likely to be annoyed by it if we do notice it**
 
• In this final part, it is mentioned that if the audience does happen to notice the product placement during the climax, there is a higher chance of them being annoyed by it. This annoyance can stem from the distraction it poses or the perception of the advertisement interrupting the narrative flow.

The sentence is discussing the effects of product placement in a narrative, and the proper order of events is:

"If a product placement appears at the climax, the moment when our attention is fixated on what will happen next, we are either less likely to notice the placement or more likely to be annoyed by it if we do notice it."

B. the feel of his hand clutching mine, his

solution:

• The **correct sequence** of these sentences is **ACBD**. Here's why:
 
• "My years in my father’s house" is the main clause, which can stand by itself as a complete sentence.
 
• **"A. **would have been unbearable had" is the start of the next part of the sentence.
 
 
• **It provides a continuation** to the main clause, implying that something made the years bearable.
 
 
 
• **"C. **I not had my brother." This sentence fits well with the previous part (A) as it provides the answer to what made the years bearable - having a brother.
 
 
• **It forms a complete and meaningful sentence** when put after A, "My years in my father’s house would have been unbearable had I not had my brother."
 
• "I never forgot" is the continuation of the first part of the sentence, focusing on the protagonist's memories related to his brother.

• This **sentence fits well **at the end as it rounds off the sentiment of the previous parts and completes the overall thought.
